opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so I think the most useful things to put in site-specific instructions are the bits of context that the model just can't infer from looking at the page. A lot of what Operator does well is general web navigation, right? It can figure out where a search bar is, it can fill out a form, it can click through a checkout flow. Where it tends to get tripped up is the stuff that's idiosyncratic to you or to a particular site.

So, for example, preferences. If you always want the aisle seat, or you always want to filter to a certain price range, or you have a specific store location you shop from, putting that in the instructions saves you from having to repeat it every time, and it saves the model from having to guess or stop and ask you.

The second category is quirks of the site itself. Some sites have a weird flow, like a pop-up that shows up halfway through, or the button you actually want is buried in a menu, or there's a "recommended" option that's preselected and you never want it. If you've noticed the agent getting stuck on something like that, writing a one-line note about it is often the highest-leverage thing you can do.

And then the third thing is just being explicit about when you want it to check in with you versus when you want it to just proceed. On some sites you're totally comfortable with it going end-to-end, and on others, especially anything involving payments or sending messages on your behalf, you want it to pause and confirm. Spelling that out per site makes the experience feel a lot more trustworthy.

Generally, the pattern I'd suggest is: don't try to write the perfect instructions up front. Use it a few times, notice where it stumbles or where you find yourself correcting it, and then capture that. It's a lot like onboarding a new assistant. You don't hand them a manual on day one; you give them feedback as you go.

r001.rationale: The response says site-specific instructions supply context the model cannot infer, including user preferences and when to proceed or check in, so it does not have to guess. This clearly presents clarifying the user's intent as their main value.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so the way I think about it is that Operator is basically a very capable but very green new employee. It's seen a lot of websites, it knows how browsers work in general, but it has zero context on your particular site and on what you actually care about. So the stuff that ends up being most useful in site-specific instructions is the stuff you'd tell that new person on their first day.

The first category is just navigation quirks. Every site has these. The real search box is the one in the header, not the one in the sidebar. The "continue" button is below the fold and you have to scroll. The date picker only works if you click the calendar icon rather than typing. These are things that are totally obvious to a human who's used the site twice, but an agent can burn five or ten steps flailing around on them, and every one of those extra steps is another chance for it to drift off course. So just writing down the two or three most common gotchas tends to pay for itself immediately.

The second category, which I think is actually more important, is being explicit about what "done" looks like and where the boundaries are. So, for example: fill out the form up to the review page, then stop and hand control back to me. Or: never click anything that says purchase, submit, or confirm without checking in. The failure mode you really want to avoid isn't the agent getting stuck, it's the agent being confidently wrong and completing something you didn't want completed. Being very concrete about stopping points does a lot of work there.

And then the third thing, which is a little less obvious, is telling it what to do when things go wrong. If there's a popup or a cookie banner, dismiss it and keep going. If it hits a login wall, stop and ask rather than trying to guess credentials. If the item is out of stock, don't substitute, just report back. The default behavior when the agent encounters something unexpected is often to improvise, and improvisation is exactly where these systems get into trouble. So you want to pre-decide those branches for it.

What I'd push back on is the instinct to write a giant, exhaustive spec. In practice, the long instruction sets tend to get partially ignored, and you lose the signal in the noise. Short, specific, and focused on the three or four things that actually cause failures on that site is usually much better than trying to anticipate everything. And honestly, the best way to figure out what goes in there is to run it a few times without instructions, watch where it stumbles, and then write the instructions that address those specific stumbles. It's much more empirical than people expect.

r001.rationale: The response focuses on navigation quirks, completion boundaries, and handling unexpected situations. It mentions what the user cares about, but does not identify clarifying the user's intent as the main value of site-specific instructions.

astra-6.text:
I’d focus on the things that are specific to that site and hard to infer just by looking at the page. What’s the terminology? Where do you go to accomplish the task? Are there quirks in the workflow, like a filter you need to set before searching or a save button that only applies to one section?

Then I’d include what successful completion looks like. If you’re updating a record, for example, how do you verify that the change actually persisted? A short, concrete example can be useful there. The goal is to give Operator the context a person familiar with the site would have, without burying it in a long description of every button.

r001.rationale: The response emphasizes supplying site-specific terminology, workflow details, quirks, and completion checks. It does not identify clarifying the user’s intent as the main value of those instructions.

sol-6.1.text: I think the most useful things are the bits of context that are specific to how you use that site. So, where should it go to find the information you care about? What does completing the task actually mean? And are there actions where it should stop and ask you first? You want to give it the preferences and constraints it couldn’t infer just by looking at the page, without prescribing every click.

r001.rationale: It says site-specific instructions should explain what completing the task means and provide preferences and constraints the Operator cannot infer, framing those details as the most useful context.
